strengths: Rigorous and novel theoretical contribution: the paper provides the first rigorous characterization of chaos and fractal convergence regions for gradient descent in a genuinely high-dimensional (matrix factorization) setting, going beyond the univariate-loss analyses of Kong & Tao (2020) and Chen et al. (2024b).

Strong and precise main results: an exact critical step size formula (Theorem 1) with a convergence region characterized up to a measure-zero set, quantified chaos (topological entropy >= log 3, periodic orbits of all periods), and a provably self-similar (degree three) fractal convergence boundary induced by l2 regularization (Theorem 3), with the unbounded interior result and small-step-size stability guarantee (Theorem 4).

The extension mechanism via the invariant orthogonal slice W and the quotient/semi-conjugacy reduction to a 2D planar map F (Propositions 2, 5, 8) is elegant and technically clean; the identity-initialization connection to deep linear/residual networks increases relevance.

The proofs (Appendices D-G) appear careful and substantive: properness, preimage structure via a quintic covering argument, conjugacy to the piecewise-linear map z -> +-3z, semi-conjugacy arguments for entropy, and use of Jelonek/Ponomarev results for the covering-map partition of the general parameter space.

Well-positioned related work, thoughtful discussion of why classical fractal-basin-boundary and chaos frameworks (Devaney, Li-Yorke, Axiom-A, Wada basins) do not directly apply, and an honest limitations section.
Supporting experiments (basin visualizations, distributional behavior, box-counting dimension ~1.249 with a clear uncertainty-exponent interpretation) and reproduction code indicated.
weaknesses: Scope limitations: the rigorous guarantees apply only to scalar factorization and, for general matrix factorization, only on a measure-thin invariant slice W of orthogonal-column initializations; chaotic dynamics under generic initialization and in deep factorization are only supported empirically (2D random slices), not proven.

The mechanistic 'covering map' explanation of chaos in Section 4 is explicitly heuristic ('we reason that chaotic phenomena arise when...'), leaving the key general mechanism without a rigorous proof.

Relevance to practical deep learning could be debated: the chaotic regime is confined to near-critical step sizes, and results concern shallow matrix factorization with diagonal (after rotation) targets; the paper mitigates this via the edge-of-stability literature but a deeper connection (e.g., implication for implicit bias in realistic regimes) is not fully developed.

The fractal dimension 1.249 is only numerically estimated from a finite-resolution box-counting regression on a projected 2D boundary; the theoretical fractal dimension of T(dD''_eta) is not established.

Some theorem conditions are restrictive (e.g., 0 < lambda <= min{(1/eta)-|y|, 1/(2eta)}, unboundedness proven only for y=0 though claimed qualitatively in general), and a few minor presentation issues (typos such as 'does note converge', 'which means that B(p) can be folded m times') remain.
The distributional implicit bias observation (Figure 2, right panel) is interesting but left largely unexplored.

strengths: Rigorous and novel contribution: the paper provides, to my knowledge, the first rigorous characterization of chaos (topological entropy ≥ log 3, periodic orbits of all periods) and of a fractal convergence region in gradient descent for a genuinely multi-dimensional (matrix factorization) setting, going beyond prior Li-Yorke chaos results that were restricted to univariate losses (Kong and Tao, 2020; Chen et al., 2024b).

The technical core is strong: the exact critical step size in Theorem 1 is derived via an elegant quotient/semi-conjugacy argument (the map T reducing the 2d-dimensional dynamics to a planar system, then conjugating the boundary dynamics to z^3 - 3z), and the self-similarity of the regularized convergence boundary (degree three, via the preimage structure of the covering map in Proposition 13) is a clean, nontrivial result.

The folding/covering-map explanation (Section 4, Proposition 30) gives a compelling mechanism connecting non-invertibility of the update map to the emergence of fractal basin boundaries, and the connection to the classical fractal basin boundary literature (McDonald et al., 1985) is well positioned.

The contrast between the unregularized case (convergence region smooth almost everywhere) and the regularized case (fractal boundary, unbounded interior, minimal/maximal distance solution selection) is a surprising and well-supported finding, with Theorem 4 giving the small-step-size regime where predictability is restored.

Experiments are appropriate and consistent with the theory, including visualization of measure-zero basins that prior work (Zhu et al., 2023) missed, box-counting dimension estimation, and additional experiments on general initialization and deep matrix factorization.
weaknesses: Scope of the rigorous results is narrower than the framing suggests: the fractal/chaos analysis for the unregularized case holds only when the trajectory is confined to the invariant slice W (orthogonality conditions), which excludes generic initializations and the low-rank setting d < dy. The behavior on the full parameter space (Figure 5) is only empirical and, notably, the convergence boundary there is non-smooth even without regularization, so the clean dichotomy (smooth unregularized vs. fractal regularized) may be an artifact of the special subspace W rather than a property of gradient descent per se.

Several key elements are heuristic or left to future work: the covering-map argument for chaos in general matrix factorization (Section 4) is explicitly not rigorous; the distributional implicit bias observation (Figure 2 right) is unanalyzed; the non-existence of dynamical invariants (Theorem 27) is only for d = 1 and its extension to d ≥ 2 is anticipated but unproven.

Practical significance is debatable: the phenomena occur at near-critical step sizes where training is on the verge of divergence; the paper does not demonstrate consequences for regimes practitioners actually use (e.g., edge-of-stability), nor connect the chaotic selection of minimizers to generalization outcomes.

Some presentation issues reduce polish: a number of typos and grammatical slips (e.g., 'This stands is contrast with', 'almost all initializations does not converge', 'the basin of with the saddle'), undefined notation in places (r vs. dy in Section 4/W definition), the reproducibility statement's URL is empty, and Theorem 4's conditions appear in compressed form that requires careful parsing.

The conditions in Theorem 3 (0 < λ ≤ min{(1/η) − |y|, 1/(2η)}) and the unboundedness result being restricted to y = 0 leave a gap between the proved statements and the empirically observed phenomena for general targets, which the paper acknowledges but does not close.

strengths: Rigorous and precise theoretical contribution: the paper derives the exact critical step size (Theorem 1) for unregularized scalar factorization, improving on the sufficient condition of Wang et al. (2022), and gives a nearly complete (up to measure-zero sets) description of the convergence region.

First rigorous characterization of a fractal convergence region in ML optimization: the self-similarity (degree three) of the projected boundary, the unbounded-interior result, and the estimated box-counting dimension (1.249) are new and carefully tied to unpredictability via the uncertainty exponent framework (Appendix B.2).

The quotient/semi-conjugacy reduction to a planar map F via the map T is an elegant technical device; the chain of results (properness, preimage structure with three branches, invariant boundaries, monotonicity of the Lyapunov-like function Q) is carried out in detail and appears sound, with the chaos results (topological entropy ≥ log 3, Devaney/Li-Yorke chaos on the boundary, periodic orbits of all periods) following from an explicit topological conjugacy to a piecewise linear degree-3 map.

Honest and careful positioning: the paper clearly delineates which classical chaos/fractal frameworks apply and which do not (non-invertibility, non-analyticity), and shows the system is not Devaney chaotic for d ≥ 2 (Proposition 19), which reflects nuance rather than overclaiming.

Good breadth of implications: extension to general matrix factorization via the forward-invariant slice W (covering identity and zero-asymmetric initialization), extension to shallow linear residual networks, non-existence of continuous dynamical invariants (Theorem 27), and a small-step-size stability threshold (Theorem 4) that contrasts chaotic and benign regimes.

The distributional experiments (Figure 2) and the general-initialization/deep-factorization experiments (Figures 5-7) support that the phenomena are not artifacts of the invariant slice, and the covering-map mechanism discussion gives a plausible, testable explanation.
Clear writing overall; main theorems are stated precisely with explicit parameter ranges, and reproducibility is addressed with detailed experimental protocols and released code.
weaknesses: The core chaotic dynamics ultimately reduce to the well-studied cubic map z^3 - 3z (conjugate to a tent map of slope 3); the resulting chaos conclusions (entropy log 3, periodic orbits) are largely a consequence of standard one-dimensional dynamics, so the mathematical novelty lies mainly in the careful reduction and geometric characterization rather than in new dynamical-systems tools.

The main theorems hold only for initializations in the invariant slice W, which requires d ≥ dy and excludes the low-rank setting; behavior under general initialization is supported only empirically, and the mechanism analysis for the general case (Section 4) is explicitly heuristic, with rigorous investigation deferred to future work.
The fractal-dimension estimate (1.249) is purely numerical (box counting over a limited scale range 1/2^2 to 1/2^8); a rigorous dimension result is not provided.

Some experimental visualizations (e.g., detecting measure-zero basins via contour level sets of final loss) are delicate and could be sensitive to numerical precision; validation of these visualization techniques is somewhat informal.

Practical relevance is limited: the setting is gradient descent with constant step size on shallow/deep linear matrix factorization; no connection is established to more realistic nonlinear network training, so the impact on mainstream deep learning practice is indirect (mostly conceptual, concerning implicit bias claims at large step sizes).

Minor presentation issues: occasional typos and grammatical slips (e.g., 'does note converge', 'gradient optimization', 'the analysis extend'), and the reproducibility statement ends with an empty URL.

strengths: Rigorous and complete characterization of the critical step size for gradient descent in (scalar) matrix factorization (Theorem 1), strictly generalizing prior convergence guarantees (e.g., Wang et al., 2022, which only covered a strict subset of the convergence region and a narrower step-size range).

First rigorous characterization of a fractal convergence region in machine learning optimization beyond univariate losses: self-similarity with degree three (via a careful quotient/semi-conjugacy argument through the map T), an entropy lower bound of log 3, periodic orbits of every period, and distributional-level chaos (Theorem 2) that rules out simple implicit-bias statements near the convergence boundary.

The proofs are deep and technically solid: the reduction to a 2D quotient dynamical system, the analysis of all inverse branches of a multi-valued map, conjugacy to a piecewise-linear map with entropy log 3, and symbolic dynamics are carried out in extensive, self-contained appendices. The connection to classical results (Devaney/Li-Yorke chaos, fractal basin boundary classification, covering maps via Jelonek/Ponomarev/Sard) is handled carefully, with explicit discussion of why classical tools do not directly apply.

Interesting and somewhat surprising findings, e.g., adding ℓ2 regularization (usually used to ensure well-behavedness) actually induces a fractal convergence boundary, and that unbounded convergence regions arise (Theorem 4). The result on non-existence of continuous dynamical invariants (imbalance not preserved at large step sizes) is a compelling negative result for the implicit-bias literature.

The mechanism analysis (folding/covering behavior of the GD update map) is insightful, and Proposition 6 gives a general (albeit partial) result for polynomial networks, suggesting broader relevance. Empirical validation on deep matrix factorization and ReLU networks on CIFAR-10 connects the theory to practice, showing a clear transition from a predictable EoS regime to a chaotic regime with sharpness spanning (γmin, 2/η), consistent with Theorem 2.
Clear writing in the main text, well-organized appendix, honest limitations section, and reproducibility statement with detailed experiment specifications.
weaknesses: Scope of the rigorous results is limited: the main theorems hold for scalar factorization and, by decoupling, for general matrix factorization only on the orthogonal-initialization subspace W. Dynamics for general initializations, deep factorization, and nonlinear-activation networks are only explored empirically; Proposition 6 shows a covering structure but does not establish the key conditions (GDη(C) ⊃ C, boundary containment) needed for chaos.

The empirical experiments (Figures 4, 5, 12, 13) are qualitative: they show sensitivity and fractal-like patterns but do not quantitatively test the theory (e.g., no measurement of topological entropy, uncertainty exponents, or verification of the predicted interval support of sharpness on real data).

Practical significance of the chaotic regime could be argued to be limited: it concerns near-critical step sizes where convergence to a minimizer is at stake, and the paper does not quantify how commonly practitioners operate in this regime; the relation to the EoS regime (which does converge) is discussed but the boundary between the regimes in realistic settings is not characterized.

Some headline claims (e.g., 'there are no simple implicit biases') are broader than what is proven, since the negative results are established for matrix factorization with orthogonal initializations and (for invariants) only for d = 1; the authors acknowledge this but the abstract phrasing is slightly stronger than the evidence.

Novelty relative to the dynamical-systems literature is primarily in the application and adaptation: the machinery (semi-conjugacy, symbolic dynamics, IFS-style self-similarity, fractal basin boundaries) is classical, and the main contribution is identifying that these structures arise in GD on matrix factorization and characterizing them exactly.

Minor presentation issues: the reproducibility statement lacks the actual URL, and some theorem statements (e.g., Theorem 4's conditions on λ relative to η and |y|) are technical and restrict the applicability in ways that are easy to miss.

strengths: Technically thorough analysis: the paper derives an exact closed-form critical step size (Theorem 1) for scalar factorization and gives a complete a.e. characterization of the convergence region, going beyond prior partial results (e.g., Wang et al., 2022, which only covers a strict subset and smaller step sizes).

The dynamical-systems toolkit is applied rigorously: a quotient/semi-conjugacy reduction to a planar map, symbolic-dynamics arguments proving Devaney/Li-Yorke chaos, a topological entropy lower bound of log 3, and a formal self-similarity (degree-three) result for the regularized convergence boundary are all non-trivial and, to my knowledge, novel for this setting.

The extension to general matrix factorization on the orthogonal-invariant subspace W, including identity initialization and linear residual networks, is clean and verified (Proposition 31, Theorems 29-30).

The writing is generally clear, related work is comprehensive, and experiments (fractal parameter-space slices, two-regime behavior of final sharpness vs. step size on CIFAR-10 subsets) qualitatively support the theory; code is promised for reproducibility.
Appendices include careful comparisons to classical chaos/fractal theory (Devaney, Li-Yorke, fractal basin boundaries) and honest clarification of which notions apply and which do not.
weaknesses: Restricted scope of the main theoretical results: the chaotic phenomena and fractal boundaries are rigorously established only for scalar factorization and, in the general case, only on the special invariant subspace W of orthogonal initializations. Dynamics under general initializations, deep factorization, and nonlinear networks are treated only empirically, so the headline claims generalize beyond what is actually proven.

Limited practical significance: the sensitivity results concern behavior in arbitrarily small neighborhoods of the convergence boundary and of measure-zero basins, and the chaos (topological entropy, Devaney/Li-Yorke) is confined to an invariant boundary set. For typical random initializations the algorithm still converges a.e. within a smooth ellipsoid, so the claim that 'there are no simple implicit biases' is arguably overstated relative to the measure-theoretic content of the theorems.

Proposition 6 (covering map for polynomial-activation networks) is only partial: it does not establish that the covered set contains itself or a basin boundary, which the authors themselves admit is the key ingredient for chaos. Its connection to the main results is therefore more suggestive than substantive.

The contribution is incremental relative to Kong and Tao (2020) and Chen et al. (2024b): the core observation that gradient descent on polynomial-like losses can be chaotic (period-doubling, Li-Yorke) is known in univariate settings, and this paper largely elevates it to a bilinear/matrix setting with quotient-map techniques; the qualitative conclusions (unpredictability at large step sizes) are not surprising.

Experiments are small-scale (25-image subsets of CIFAR-10, depth-3 networks, single random initializations per panel) and exclusively full-batch GD (no SGD), which limits the external validity of the empirical claims of a 'chaotic regime' in realistic training.

The absence of SGD/momentum/stochastic variants in the theory is a notable gap, since the audience most interested in step-size phenomena trains with stochastic methods; the empirical momentum results are not matched by analysis.

Several notable results (unbounded convergence region when y=0, non-existence of continuous invariants in Appendix F) hold only for d=1, yet are highlighted in the main narrative without sufficiently clear caveats.

strengths: Significant and clearly articulated contribution: the paper provides the first rigorous characterization of chaotic dynamics and fractal convergence regions for gradient descent in a genuinely high-dimensional (multivariate) optimization setting, going beyond the univariate loss analyses of Kong and Tao (2020) and Chen et al. (2024b).

Technically strong and apparently complete results: an exact closed-form critical step size (Theorem 1) with a full almost-everywhere characterization of the convergence region, positive topological entropy (h >= log 3), periodic orbits of all periods, and a proof that the projected convergence boundary is self-similar with degree three (Theorem 4). The reduction of the dynamics to a 2D quotient system via the fiber map T is elegant and powerful.

Novel and somewhat surprising message: adding L2 regularization makes the global dynamics less predictable (fractal convergence boundary), and large step sizes destroy simple implicit biases (balancedness, distance-minimization, dynamical invariants), which is a meaningful counterpoint to the existing large-learning-rate implicit-bias literature.

The proposed mechanism (multi-fold covering/folding behavior of the GD update map) is well motivated, supported by Proposition 6 for polynomial-activation networks, and clearly laid out as an agenda for extending chaos analysis beyond matrix factorization.

Comprehensive supporting material: extensive appendices with careful, detailed proofs; thorough positioning relative to Edge of Stability, catapult, and chaos literature; and experiments on deep matrix factorization and ReLU networks on CIFAR-10 that exhibit both EoS and chaotic regimes consistent with the theory (Theorem 2 predicting final sharpness spanning nearly all values below 2/eta).
Honest scope discussion: limitations, future directions, and a careful appendix comparing Devaney/Li-Yorke chaos notions and classical fractal basin boundary theory are provided.
weaknesses: The core rigorous results are confined to a restricted setting: scalar factorization, and for the general matrix factorization case, only to the invariant orthogonal subspace W (which includes identity initialization). Dynamics outside W are characterized only empirically or via transient-chaos heuristics, so the title's broad framing ('matrix factorization') somewhat overstates the proven scope.

Some headline quantities are less conclusive than they appear: the entropy lower bound log 3 and periodic-orbit results follow from a semi-conjugacy to the cubic map z^3 - 3z restricted to a measure-zero boundary; the paper itself shows the full system is not Devaney chaotic for d >= 2. The practical relevance of chaos concentrated on null sets could be questioned, though Theorem 2 partially addresses this at the distributional level.

The neural network experiments (Figures 4-5, 12-13) are small-scale (depth-3 MLP, 2-class 25-image subsets of CIFAR-10, fixed random slices) and are qualitative evidence only; there is no quantitative validation (e.g., measured Lyapunov exponents, uncertainty exponents) in the deep-learning setting.

Proposition 6 (covering map property for polynomial networks) does not establish the key ingredients (invariance of a basin boundary, folding onto itself), so the extension path from matrix factorization to general networks remains speculative.

Reproducibility statement is incomplete in the submission: the code URL appears blank; experiment details, while present, rely on package-specific visualization procedures (contour-based basin extraction) whose precision is not quantified (e.g., confidence interval on the 1.249 box-counting dimension estimate is not reported).

Novelty is partly incremental relative to prior rigorous chaos analyses in gradient descent (Kong & Tao 2020; Chen et al. 2024b); the main novelty is the dimensional and structural extension (quotient dynamics, self-similarity of the boundary, regularization-induced fractality), which some reviewers may view as a specialized setting.
